transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: City officials in San Francisco have announced a new plan to expand the city's public transportation network with the introduction of electric bus rapid transit lines along major commuter routes. The project, which is expected to begin construction early next year, will create dedicated bus lanes that allow electric buses to travel faster than regular traffic, reducing commute times by an estimated 30 percent for thousands of daily riders. The new fleet of buses will be fully electric, producing zero emissions and helping the city meet its climate goals of reducing carbon emissions by 40 percent within the next decade. Transit authorities also plan to upgrade bus stops with real-time arrival information, improved lighting, and seating for waiting passengers. The project is being funded through a combination of city transportation bonds and a federal grant for sustainable infrastructure. City leaders say the expanded bus rapid transit system will not only make commuting easier but also help reduce traffic congestion and improve air quality in neighborhoods along the routes.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: A new national survey on teenage reading habits has revealed some concerning trends among young people in the United Kingdom. The study, conducted by the National Literacy Trust, surveyed over 40,000 secondary school students aged 11 to 16 across England, Scotland, and Wales. Researchers found that only 32 percent of teenagers reported reading for pleasure on a daily basis, down from 38 percent just five years ago. The survey also found that nearly one in five teenagers said they rarely or never read in their free time, preferring instead to spend time on social media, playing video games, or watching streaming services. However, there was a positive finding as well: teenagers who read for pleasure reported significantly higher levels of mental well-being and life satisfaction compared to their non-reading peers. The National Literacy Trust is calling on schools and parents to work together to promote reading by providing access to a wider variety of books and creating dedicated reading time both at school and at home.
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Scientists are warning that declining bee populations across North America and Europe could have serious consequences for global food production and ecosystem health. Over the past fifteen years, bee populations have decreased by approximately 30 percent each decade, a trend that researchers attribute to several interconnected factors including habitat loss, pesticide use, climate change, and the spread of parasitic mites. Bees play a critical role in agriculture by pollinating approximately 75 percent of global food crops, including fruits, vegetables, and nuts. Without sufficient bee populations, farmers would face significantly lower crop yields, potentially leading to higher food prices and reduced availability of nutritious foods. Environmental groups are urging governments to implement stricter regulations on certain pesticides known to be harmful to bees, as well as fund programs to create wildflower habitats and support sustainable farming practices. Some farmers have already begun taking action by planting hedgerows and wildflower strips along their fields to provide food and shelter for bee populations.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Laura): Hi, Mark. I heard you're moving to a new apartment next month. How's the house-hunting going?

Man (Mark): It's been a bit stressful, actually. I've looked at about six places so far, but nothing has felt quite right. I need somewhere that's closer to my new office in the city centre, but rent prices there are so high.

Woman: I know what you mean. I was looking at places in the centre last year, and I couldn't believe how expensive they were. Have you considered sharing a flat with a roommate? That could cut your costs significantly.
Man: I have thought about it, but I've been living alone for three years now, and I'm used to having my own space. I'm not sure I want to deal with sharing a kitchen and bathroom again.

Woman: That's understandable. What about neighborhoods just outside the centre? They're usually cheaper, and if you're near a tube station, the commute isn't too bad. I live in West Hampstead, and it takes me only 15 minutes on the Jubilee line to get to work.
Man: That's actually a good idea. I've been focusing too much on being right in the centre. What's the rent like in areas like that?
Woman: I pay 1,200 pounds a month for a one-bedroom flat, which is about 400 pounds less than similar places in Zone 1. And my neighborhood has great shops, cafes, and a lovely park nearby.
Man: That sounds really nice. I think I'll start looking at places in Zones 2 and 3. Do you have any other tips for finding a good flat?

Woman: Definitely start checking online listings now, and set up alerts so you get notified when new places become available. Also, be prepared to act quickly—good flats get rented within days. And make sure you have all your documents ready: proof of income, references from previous landlords, and a deposit.

Man: Thanks for the advice, Laura. I'll start expanding my search this weekend. Would you mind if I asked you to come look at a place with me if I find one I like? A second opinion would be really helpful.
Woman: Of course! I'd be happy to help. Just let me know when you find something promising.

paras: Woman (Sarah): Hey, Jason. Are you still working at the coffee shop on weekends? I thought you were going to look for something different this semester.

Woman: That's awesome! A bookstore sounds like the perfect part-time job for you since you love reading so much. What will your hours be?

Man: I'm working 10 AM to 4 PM every Saturday and 12 PM to 5 PM on Sundays. It's similar to what I was doing at the coffee shop, but the hourly wage is two dollars higher, and they give employees a 30 percent discount on all books.

Man: I saw a help-wanted sign in the window when I was browsing there last month. I filled out an application right there, and they called me for an interview last week. I met with the store manager, and we talked about books for, like, 45 minutes. I think that's why I got hired—we had similar taste in novels.

I only have classes on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, so I have plenty of time during the week to study and get homework done. Working weekends keeps me from wasting too much time watching television or scrolling on my phone anyway.

Man: Definitely! I get off at 5 PM on Sundays, so I can make our 6:30 study sessions no problem. I'm really looking forward to starting next week.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Female)
paras: The COVID-19 pandemic dramatically accelerated a trend that was already underway: the shift toward remote work and flexible working arrangements. While working from home was once considered a rare perk offered by only a few forward-thinking companies, it has now become a standard option for millions of workers around the world. As we move beyond the pandemic, it is clear that remote work is here to stay in some form, bringing with it both significant benefits and notable challenges.

One of the most frequently cited advantages of remote work is increased flexibility. Without a daily commute, workers gain back valuable time that can be spent with family, pursuing hobbies, or simply getting more sleep. Many people also report being more productive when working from home, as they experience fewer interruptions from colleagues and can create a workspace tailored to their personal preferences. Employers benefit too—companies that offer remote work options often see reduced overhead costs for office space and utilities, and they can hire talented employees from anywhere in the world rather than being limited to a specific geographic area.

However, remote work also has its drawbacks. Many employees struggle with feelings of isolation and loneliness when they don't have regular in-person interactions with colleagues. The boundary between work life and home life can also become blurred, leading to longer working hours and increased burnout. New employees, in particular, may find it difficult to integrate into company culture and build relationships with coworkers when they rarely meet face to face. Communication can sometimes be less effective remotely, as nuances can be lost in emails and instant messages that would be easily picked up in in-person conversations.

As companies navigate this new landscape, many are adopting hybrid models that allow employees to split their time between working in the office and working from home. This approach aims to capture the best of both worlds—the flexibility of remote work combined with the collaboration and social connection of in-person work. Ultimately, the future of work will likely involve a variety of arrangements, as companies and employees continue to experiment and find what works best for their individual needs.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Male)
paras: Food waste has become a massive global problem with significant environmental, economic, and social consequences. According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, approximately one-third of all food produced worldwide for human consumption is wasted every year—that's roughly 1.3 billion tons of food. This waste occurs at every stage of the food supply chain, from farms and processing facilities to grocery stores, restaurants, and individual households.

The environmental impact of food waste is staggering. When food is thrown away and ends up in landfills, it decomposes and produces methane, a greenhouse gas that is approximately 25 times more potent than carbon dioxide in terms of trapping heat in the atmosphere. In fact, global food waste is estimated to contribute about 8 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions. Additionally, the resources that went into producing that food—water, land, energy, and labor—are essentially wasted as well. For example, producing one kilogram of beef requires roughly 15,000 liters of water; when that beef is thrown away, all that water is wasted too.

Economically, food waste costs households, businesses, and governments hundreds of billions of dollars each year. The average family in a developed country throws away hundreds of dollars worth of food annually. Grocery stores lose money when they discard produce that doesn't meet strict cosmetic standards, and restaurants waste food through oversized portions and inflexible purchasing practices. Meanwhile, nearly 800 million people around the world suffer from chronic hunger, meaning food waste is also a moral issue—perfectly good food is being discarded while many people cannot afford enough to eat.

Addressing food waste requires action at every level. Farms can improve harvesting practices to reduce crop losses. Grocery stores can relax cosmetic standards for produce and donate unsold but safe-to-eat food rather than throwing it away. Restaurants can offer smaller portion options and donate leftover food to local food banks. At the household level, consumers can plan meals better, learn how to store food properly, understand expiration dates, and compost food scraps rather than throwing them in the trash. Many countries have already begun implementing policies to reduce food waste, including tax incentives for food donation and laws requiring businesses to separate food waste for composting. While there is no single solution, reducing food waste by even half would have enormous benefits for the planet and for people around the world.

20. What environmental problem is caused by food decomposing in landfills?

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Male)
paras: For many people, pets are more than just animals—they are beloved members of the family. But beyond the joy and companionship that pets provide, research has shown that owning a pet can actually have significant benefits for human physical and mental health.

One of the most well-documented health benefits of pet ownership is improved cardiovascular health. Numerous studies have found that pet owners, particularly dog owners, tend to have lower blood pressure, lower cholesterol levels, and reduced risk of heart disease compared to non-pet owners. This is likely due in part to the fact that dog owners typically get more regular physical activity from walking their dogs. Walking a dog for just 30 minutes a day adds up to 3.5 hours of extra exercise per week, which meets recommended physical activity guidelines for adults.

Pets also have remarkable effects on mental health and emotional well-being. Interacting with animals has been shown to reduce levels of cortisol, the body's primary stress hormone, while increasing the release of serotonin and dopamine, neurotransmitters associated with feelings of calm and happiness. Many people find that simply petting a cat or dog can help them feel more relaxed after a difficult day. Pets also provide constant companionship and unconditional love, which can be especially valuable for people living alone, elderly individuals, or those going through challenging times such as bereavement or job loss.

Therapy animals are now commonly used in hospitals, nursing homes, schools, and even workplaces to help reduce stress and anxiety. In hospital settings, visits from therapy dogs have been shown to reduce patients' need for pain medication and speed up recovery times after surgery. For children with autism spectrum disorder or other developmental challenges, working with specially trained animals can help improve social skills and reduce anxiety. In universities, therapy dog programs during exam season have become increasingly popular as a way to help students manage stress.

However, it is important to note that pet ownership is not for everyone. Owning a pet is a significant responsibility that requires time, money, and commitment. Pets need food, veterinary care, attention, and exercise every day for their entire lives, which can be 10 to 15 years or more for dogs and cats. Potential pet owners should carefully consider their lifestyle, living situation, and ability to care for an animal before bringing one into their home. For those who are ready for the responsibility, though, the health benefits and companionship that pets provide can make pet ownership one of life's most rewarding experiences.
